displayQuote: Every adversity has the seed of an equivalent or greater benefit

meta.title: Who really said "Every adversity has the seed of an equivalent or greater benefit"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Napoleon Hill wrote the thought, but not quite in these words. Think and Grow Rich (first published 1937) says “equivalent advantage” — here is where the popular wording comes from.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Every adversity has the seed of an equivalent or greater benefit'?
meta.ogDescription: Napoleon Hill wrote the thought, but not quite in these words. Think and Grow Rich (first published 1937) says “equivalent advantage”. Where the popular wording comes from.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: The idea is unmistakably Hill’s, but this exact sentence is not how his famous book puts it. Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ traces this wording to Success Through a Positive Mental Attitude (1960), the book Hill co-wrote with W. Clement Stone, at Ch. 14, p. 222 — citing it there as a maxim of Hill’s. We could not open that page to confirm it: the Internet Archive’s copy is lending-restricted and its search-inside API refused the query. What we could read in full is Think and Grow Rich — first published in 1937 — and it phrases the same idea differently. The Internet Archive scans we searched carry no edition statement, so we can tell you what the book’s text reads, not which printing we read.

source.heading: Where the wording comes from

docMeta.dd: Success Through a Positive Mental Attitude
Napoleon Hill and W. Clement Stone
Ch. 14, p. 222 — per Wikiquote; not independently read

source.excerpt: Despite the fact that all the philosophy I had examined clearly indicated that EVERY ADVERSITY BRINGS WITH IT THE SEED OF AN EQUIVALENT ADVANTAGE, I must confess that I had not the slightest idea how this affliction could ever become an asset.
trail: The circulating wording is documented: Wikiquote ↗ lists it in its sourced section and cites it to Success Through a Positive Mental Attitude (1960) by Hill and W. Clement Stone, Ch. 14, p. 222, describing it as a maxim of Hill’s.

We tried and failed to confirm that page ourselves. The Internet Archive’s 1960 edition ↗ is a controlled-lending item; its search-inside API returned HTTP 403, so the locator above is Wikiquote’s, not ours.

We did read Think and Grow Rich end to end, in a scanned copy on the Internet Archive ↗, and searched its full text. That scan states no edition, so this establishes what the book says rather than which printing it is. The words “equivalent or greater benefit” do not occur anywhere in it; Hill’s recurring formulations are “EVERY ADVERSITY BRINGS WITH IT THE SEED OF AN EQUIVALENT ADVANTAGE” and “EVERY FAILURE BRINGS WITH IT THE SEED OF AN EQUIVALENT SUCCESS”. A second, independent scan of the same book gave the same result.
source.excerptNote: From Think and Grow Rich, quoted from an Internet Archive scan. The small capitals are Hill’s own emphasis, reproduced identically in both scanned copies we read; neither scan identifies its printing. Note the wording: brings with it and equivalent advantage, not has and equivalent or greater benefit.

sourceLink.text: Wikiquote’s sourced entry for Napoleon Hill

source.rightsNote: Both candidate sources are modern books — Think and Grow Rich (1937) and Success Through a Positive Mental Attitude (1960) — so neither is in the US public domain. Hill founded the Napoleon Hill Foundation ↗ in 1963, and it administers his work. The excerpt above is quoted here for commentary and identification.

author.name: Napoleon Hill
author.heading: About Napoleon Hill
author.bio: Oliver Napoleon Hill was an American self-help author whose Think and Grow Rich (1937) became one of the best-selling books of its kind. He founded the Napoleon Hill Foundation in 1963. Readers should know that the authenticity of many of Hill’s claims about his own life has been widely disputed — his celebrated collaboration with Andrew Carnegie, the origin story of his entire philosophy, remains unsupported by any evidence.

misattribution.heading: The wording drifted
misattribution.intro: Nobody else is being credited here — Hill really is the author. What has drifted is the sentence itself.

items.why: This sentence is routinely quoted as if it were the line from Hill’s best-known book. It is not. We searched the complete text of a scanned copy of the book ↗ and confirmed the phrase “equivalent or greater benefit” appears nowhere in it. Hill’s book says “EVERY ADVERSITY BRINGS WITH IT THE SEED OF AN EQUIVALENT ADVANTAGE”.

misattribution.truthLine: The shorter, smoother version people quote is documented — Wikiquote ↗ places it in the 1960 book Hill co-wrote with W. Clement Stone, not in Think and Grow Rich.

context.heading: Why the two versions differ
lead: Hill spent thirty years restating the same handful of maxims for new audiences, and the sentences got shorter and smoother each time. Think and Grow Rich buries this one inside a confession of doubt — Hill admits he had “not the slightest idea” how his own affliction could ever become an asset. By 1960, writing with the insurance magnate W. Clement Stone, it had been polished into a standalone motto.

That is the ordinary life of an aphorism, and it is worth knowing which version you are quoting. If you attribute the smooth one to Think and Grow Rich, you are citing a book that does not contain it.

An Internet Archive scan of Think and Grow Rich reads "EVERY ADVERSITY BRINGS WITH IT THE SEED OF AN EQUIVALENT ADVANTAGE" and does not contain the phrase "equivalent or greater benefit". The scan carries no edition statement.
Success Through a Positive Mental Attitude by Napoleon Hill, catalogued with date 1960, exists as a controlled-lending item on the Internet Archive.

Hill founded the Napoleon Hill Foundation in 1963, and the authenticity of many of his claims — including his collaboration with Andrew Carnegie — has been widely disputed and remains unsupported by evidence.
